facts.claim: Kirchenbauer et al. (2023) mark a model’s text by using the previous token and a secret key to split the vocabulary at random into green and red lists, then softly favouring green tokens; anyone with the key can check text without the model.
Kirchenbauer et al. call text marked when its green count sits more than 4 standard deviations above chance (z above 4), a false-alarm chance of 3 in 100,000.
Kirchenbauer et al. (2023), marking 200-token texts from the OPT-1.3B model, found a trade-off: settings that made the mark stronger also made the text less likely in a larger model’s judgement.
In the same tests, Kirchenbauer et al. found a small green list, a tenth of all tokens, gave the best balance of mark strength and text quality of the settings they tried.
Kirchenbauer et al. detect the mark in as few as 25 tokens, but text with few choices (low entropy) needs more; their average case needed about 128 tokens to reach z = 4.
Kirchenbauer et al. found automatic paraphrasing lowers the mark’s strength, while swapping 10% of spans barely changed detection.
Sadasivan et al. (2023, TMLR) showed repeated paraphrasing defeats watermark and other AI-text detectors with little loss of quality, and that a watermark can be spoofed onto human text.
Liang et al. (2023) found popular AI-text detectors consistently misclassified essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated, while judging native writers’ essays accurately.
Google DeepMind’s SynthID-Text (Dathathri et al., Nature, October 2024) watermarks Gemini’s replies; in a live test on nearly 20 million responses, users rated marked and unmarked replies the same.

Google DeepMind’s SynthID page (checked 30 October 2026) says SynthID marks text from the Gemini app, AI images and video, and audio from Lyria and NotebookLM; its SynthID Detector portal (2025) checks images, video and audio from Google and partners such as OpenAI and NVIDIA.
The C2PA specification (version 2.5, October 2026) bundles statements about a file into a digitally signed claim, tied to a hash (a fingerprint) of the file’s content so any change to it shows.
OpenAI’s help page on C2PA in its images (updated September 2025) says the label can easily be removed, by accident or on purpose: most social sites strip it from uploads, and a screenshot can too.
IPTC’s digital source type “trainedAlgorithmicMedia” means media created using generative AI, the value C2PA labels use to say a file was made by a model.

The European Commission says (July 2026) the EU AI Act’s Article 50 requires AI-made content to be marked in a machine-readable, detectable way from 2 August 2026; systems already on the market before then have until 2 December 2026.
